discovery: Quantum key distribution: the invention of quantum cryptography, whose security rests on the laws of physics

nominees.name: Charles H. Bennett
nominees.affiliation: IBM Research, Thomas J. Watson Research Center, Yorktown Heights, USA

nominees.name: Artur K. Ekert
nominees.affiliation: University of Oxford, UK, and Centre for Quantum Technologies, National University of Singapore

subfield: Quantum optics and quantum information (quantum communication)
motivation: Bennett and Brassard (BB84) showed that the quantum properties of single photons, namely the no-cloning theorem and the disturbance caused by measurement, allow two parties to establish a secret key whose security follows from physics rather than computational assumptions. Ekert (E91) independently linked key security to entanglement and violation of Bell inequalities, which founded device-independent cryptography and certified randomness. These ideas turned foundational quantum mechanics into a new technology. QKD has since been demonstrated over fibre networks, through turbulent free-space links in daylight, and between orbiting satellites and ground stations across continents, and it is now being deployed in national and European quantum communication infrastructures. Few conceptual advances in physics have created a whole experimental field and an industry. The 2022 prize recognised entanglement experiments; the inventors of quantum cryptography deserve recognition for opening the era of quantum-secured communication.
